sessions.title: Characteristics of Living Things
indicators: Identify living and non-living things in the environment
State the characteristics of living things (they grow, breathe, eat, move, reproduce, respond to stimuli)
Distinguish between living and non-living things by observation
Work in pairs to sort pictures into living and non-living groups (collaboration)
Use digital slideshows or short videos to explore living things (digital literacy)
Develop respect for all living things (personal development)
sessions.content:
Alive or Not? – The World Around Us

Everything around us can be grouped into living things and non-living things. Living things are alive. Non-living things are not.

1. What Living Things Do

All living things do these things:

  • Grow: A chick grows into a hen. A small seed grows into a big tree.
  • Breathe: We breathe air. Fish breathe in water.
  • Eat (feed): A goat eats grass. We eat kenkey, rice, fruits.
  • Move: A bird flies. A snake crawls. A child runs.
  • Reproduce (have young ones): A dog gives birth to puppies. A hen lays eggs.
  • Respond to things around them (sensitivity): When you touch a hot object, you pull your hand away. A plant grows towards the light.

Examples of living things: boy, girl, cat, mango tree, maize plant, fish, butterfly, ant, mushroom.

Examples of non-living things: stone, water, pencil, desk, car, book, ball, sand.

Activity 1 – Living or non-living walk
Walk around the school compound. Point to five living and five non-living things. Say why each is living or non-living. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Picture sort with checklist
In pairs, sort picture cards into two hoops labelled 'Living' and 'Non-Living'. Use a simple checklist: Does it grow? Does it need food? Does it move by itself? (collaboration).

Digital corner: Watch a short animated video on a tablet showing a seed growing into a plant and a chick hatching. Discuss: What shows that these are living? (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.1

  1. Name three living things you see on your way to school.
  2. Write two reasons why a stone is non-living.
  3. Draw a living thing and a non-living thing. Label them.
  4. Why does a car move but it is not a living thing? Explain.

sessions.title: Plants in Our Environment
indicators: Identify common plants in the locality (mango, maize, cassava, flowers)
Describe the external parts of a plant: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits
Explain simple functions: roots hold the plant and absorb water, stem supports, leaves make food
Work in groups to observe and draw a local plant (collaboration)
Use digital plant identification apps or resources (digital literacy)
Appreciate the importance of plants for food, medicine and shade (personal development)
sessions.content:
Green Helpers – Plants

Plants are living things. They are very important because they give us food, medicine, wood and the air we breathe.

1. Parts of a Plant

  • Roots: Hold the plant firmly in the soil. They take in water and nutrients. Examples: carrot, cassava (we eat some roots).
  • Stem: Supports the plant. It carries water and food between roots and leaves. Examples: sugar cane, plantain stem.
  • Leaves: Make food for the plant using sunlight. This is called photosynthesis (simple term: the plant's kitchen). Example: cocoyam leaf, mango leaf.
  • Flowers: Make seeds and fruits. They are often colourful to attract insects and birds. Examples: hibiscus, rose.
  • Fruits: Protect the seeds. We eat many fruits. Examples: orange, mango, tomato, pepper, okra.

Activity 1 – Pull and observe a weed
Gently pull out a small weed or grass. Wash the roots. Observe all the parts: roots, stem, leaves. If there is a flower or fruit, note them. Draw and label. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Plant part salad
Bring different parts of plants we eat: carrot (root), sugar cane (stem), lettuce (leaf), cauliflower (flower), tomato (fruit). Sort them and discuss. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a plant identification app like 'PlantNet' or a picture gallery to see different local plants and their parts. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.2

  1. Draw a plant and label its roots, stem, leaves, flower and fruit.
  2. What job do the roots do? Write one sentence.
  3. Name two fruits and two vegetables we eat that come from plants.
  4. What part of the plant makes food? Where does it happen?

sessions.title: Animals in the Local Environment
indicators: Name common domestic and wild animals found in Ghana
Classify animals by where they live: land, water, air
Describe how different animals move (walk, fly, swim, crawl, hop)
Work in groups to create an animal movement game (collaboration, creativity)
Use digital animal encyclopedias or apps to learn about animal habitats (digital literacy)
Show concern for the welfare of animals (personal development)
sessions.content:
Animals Big and Small

Animals are living things. They are found everywhere – on land, in water and in the air. Ghana has many different animals.

1. Where Animals Live

  • Land animals: dog, goat, cat, cow, lion, elephant, snake, lizard, ant.
  • Water animals (aquatic): fish, crab, tilapia, crocodile, octopus, frog (lives in water and on land).
  • Air animals (that fly): eagle, parrot, bat (it flies), butterfly, housefly, mosquito.

2. How Animals Move

Animals move in different ways:

  • Walk or run: dog, goat, cow, elephant.
  • Fly: bird, butterfly, mosquito.
  • Swim: fish, frog, crocodile.
  • Crawl: snake, lizard, snail.
  • Hop or jump: frog, grasshopper, kangaroo (not local but known).

Activity 1 – Move like an animal
Teacher calls out an animal. Pupils move like that animal: 'Fly like a bird!' 'Crawl like a snake!' 'Hop like a frog!' (creativity).

Activity 2 – Habitat sorting
Place three large circles labelled 'Land', 'Water', 'Air' on the floor. In groups, sort animal picture cards into the correct circle. Discuss any that could belong in two. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use an interactive animal atlas app to explore an animal's habitat. Tap to see a video of how it moves. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.1

  1. Name two animals that live on land, two in water and two that fly.
  2. How does a fish move? How does a bird move?
  3. Draw a frog and write one sentence about where it lives.
  4. Why can't a fish live on land? Give one reason.

sessions.title: What Animals Eat and Food Chains
indicators: Identify animals as plant-eaters (herbivores), meat-eaters (carnivores) and both (omnivores)
Give examples of each type of eater
Draw a simple food chain (e.g., grass -> grasshopper -> bird)
Work in pairs to sort animals by what they eat (collaboration)
Use digital interactive food chain games (digital literacy)
Understand that all animals depend on plants or other animals for food (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Who Eats What? – Animal Diets

Animals eat different foods. Some eat only plants, some eat only meat, and some eat both plants and meat.

1. Types of Eaters

  • Herbivores (plant-eaters): goat (grass), cow (grass), rabbit (carrots, leaves), grasshopper (leaves).
  • Carnivores (meat-eaters): lion (meat), cat (rats, fish), eagle (snakes, small birds), dog (meat, bones).
  • Omnivores (eat both): hen (grains, insects), pig (anything), human (rice, fish, meat), rat (grains, insects).

2. Simple Food Chain

A food chain shows who eats whom. It starts with a plant. Example: Grass is eaten by a grasshopper. The grasshopper is eaten by a bird. We draw: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Bird.

Activity 1 – Food sorting race
In pairs, you receive a set of animal picture cards. Sort them into three hoops: Herbivore, Carnivore, Omnivore. Check with another pair. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Build a food chain
Use cards or drawings to build a simple food chain: Leaf -> Snail -> Chicken. Pupils hold cards and stand in a line. Discuss what would happen if one part disappeared. (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Play an online food chain game where you drag organisms into the correct order. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.2

  1. Write if each animal is a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore: cow, lion, chicken.
  2. Why can't a lion eat grass? Explain.
  3. Draw a food chain that includes a plant, an insect and a bird.
  4. What do we call animals that eat both plants and meat? Give one example.

sessions.title: External Body Parts and Their Functions
indicators: Name major external body parts: head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, neck, arms, hands, fingers, legs, feet, toes
State the function of each major body part
Participate in action songs and labelling activities
Work in pairs to trace and label a body outline (collaboration)
Use interactive body labelling apps to reinforce learning (digital literacy)
Appreciate the need to protect all body parts (personal development)
sessions.content:
My Wonderful Body – Parts I Can See

Our body has many parts on the outside. Each part helps us do something special.

1. Body Parts and Their Jobs

  • Head: Contains the brain for thinking and control.
  • Eyes: Help us see things around us. We have two eyes.
  • Ears: Help us hear sounds – music, voices, warnings.
  • Nose: Helps us breathe and smell different things.
  • Mouth: For eating, talking, smiling. Contains teeth and tongue.
  • Neck: Connects head to the body, allows head to turn.
  • Arms and hands: For holding, writing, carrying, throwing.
  • Fingers: Help us grasp small objects, write, draw.
  • Legs and feet: For standing, walking, running, jumping, kicking.
  • Toes: Help with balance.

Activity 1 – Head, shoulders, knees and toes
Sing the action song with movements. Speed up each round. (creativity).

Activity 2 – Body tracing and labelling
In pairs, one pupil lies on a large sheet of paper. The partner traces the outline. Then both label as many external body parts as they can. Display. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a body labelling app where you drag the name to the correct body part. Listen to the part spoken aloud. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.1

  1. Draw a picture of yourself. Label your head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, arms, hands, legs and feet.
  2. What do you use your ears for? Write a sentence.
  3. Which body part helps you pick up a pencil?
  4. Why should we protect our eyes? Give one reason.

sessions.title: Keeping Healthy – Cleanliness, Food and Exercise
indicators: Explain why personal hygiene is important (hand washing, bathing, brushing teeth)
Identify healthy foods and the need for a balanced diet
Explain the importance of exercise, rest and sleep
Work in groups to create a healthy habits poster (collaboration, creativity)
Use digital resources to track daily health routines (digital literacy)
Take responsibility for personal health (personal development)
sessions.content:
Stay Strong and Well

A healthy body helps us learn, play and grow. We must keep clean, eat good food, exercise and rest.

1. Cleanliness (Personal Hygiene)

  • Wash hands with soap and water: before eating, after using the toilet, after playing, after touching animals. This removes germs that cause sickness.
  • Bathe every day to keep skin clean and fresh.
  • Brush teeth twice a day – morning and night – to prevent tooth decay and bad breath.
  • Keep nails short and clean to avoid dirt and germs.

2. Healthy Eating

Eat a variety of foods from the three main groups:

  • Energy-giving foods: rice, maize, yam, cassava, bread.
  • Body-building foods: fish, meat, eggs, beans, groundnuts.
  • Protective foods: fruits (orange, banana, pawpaw), vegetables (kontomire, garden eggs, tomatoes).

Drink plenty of clean water every day. Limit sweets, biscuits and sugary drinks.

3. Exercise, Rest and Sleep

Play and exercise every day (running, football, ampe, dancing). Exercise makes the heart, muscles and bones strong. Sleep early and get about 9-10 hours of rest so the body can repair and grow.

Activity 1 – Healthy plate drawing
Draw a plate and fill it with food from each group for a healthy lunch. Label the foods. (creativity).

Activity 2 – Healthy habits checklist
In groups, make a weekly chart with these daily tasks: I washed my hands before eating. I brushed my teeth. I exercised or played outside. I slept early. Tick each day you complete all. (collaboration, personal development).

Digital corner: Use a simple habit-tracking app or take photos of your healthy meals and share with the class. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.2

  1. Write three times when you must wash your hands.
  2. Name one energy-giving food, one body-building food and one protective food.
  3. Why is exercise important? Give one reason.
  4. Draw a poster showing two ways to keep your body clean.

sessions.title: Exploring Materials – Wood, Metal, Plastic, Glass, Fabric
indicators: Identify common materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper, clay
Describe the properties of these materials (hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, waterproof, transparent)
Match materials to objects made from them
Work in groups to sort objects by material (collaboration)
Use digital material property games (digital literacy)
Appreciate the use of different materials in everyday life (personal development)
sessions.content:
What Is It Made Of? – Materials Around Us

Everything we use is made from a material. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper and clay are common materials.

1. Properties of Materials

  • Wood: Hard, can be rough or smooth. Used for chairs, tables, doors. Comes from trees.
  • Metal: Hard, strong, shiny, often cold to touch. Used for pots, cutlery, roofing sheets, cars.
  • Plastic: Light, can be hard or flexible, waterproof. Used for buckets, bottles, toys, bags.
  • Glass: Hard, smooth, transparent (you can see through it), breaks easily. Used for windows, mirrors, drinking cups.
  • Fabric (cloth): Soft, flexible. Used for clothes, curtains, bags.
  • Paper: Light, flexible, tears easily. Made from trees. Used for books, writing, packaging.
  • Clay: Found in soil, can be moulded and baked to become hard. Used for pots, bricks, bowls.

Activity 1 – Material detectives
Walk around the classroom. Touch different objects. Say: 'This desk is made of wood. It is hard and smooth.' 'The window is glass. It is transparent.' (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Sorting by material
Collect a variety of small objects. In groups, sort them into piles by material: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric. Discuss why certain objects are made from a particular material. (collaboration, critical thinking).

Digital corner: Play an online game where you click on an object and identify its material. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.1

  1. Name the material: a chair made from a tree. A bottle that you can see through.
  2. Why are cooking pots usually made of metal? Write one reason.
  3. Draw two objects made of plastic. Label them.
  4. Which material is soft and used for clothes? Write its name.

sessions.title: Understanding Push and Pull
indicators: Define push as moving something away from you, pull as moving something towards you
Give everyday examples of pushing and pulling
Investigate how different objects move with a push or pull
Work in pairs to experiment with pushing and pulling toys and objects (collaboration)
Use digital animations showing forces in action (digital literacy)
Recognise that we use forces to do work (personal development)
sessions.content:
Move It! – Push and Pull

A force is a push or a pull. Forces make things move, stop or change direction.

1. What Are Push and Pull?

  • Push: You use force to move something away from your body. Examples: pushing a door open, pushing a wheelbarrow, pushing a chair under the desk.
  • Pull: You use force to move something towards your body. Examples: pulling a rope, pulling a drawer open, pulling a toy car with a string.

Some actions involve both push and pull: opening a door (push or pull depending on the side).

Activity 1 – Push and pull station
Set up stations with different objects: a toy car, a ball, a chair, a door, a zipper. In pairs, explore: Does it move with a push, a pull, or both? Record your findings. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Push-pull charades
A pupil acts out an action (e.g., sweeping – push, opening a drawer – pull). Others guess and say whether it is a push or pull. (creativity).

Digital corner: Watch an animated video showing children playing with different objects and how forces make them move. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.1

  1. Is kicking a ball a push or a pull? Explain.
  2. Name one thing you push at school and one thing you pull.
  3. Draw a picture of a child pulling a wagon. Label it 'pull'.
  4. Can you think of an action that uses both push and pull? Describe it.

sessions.title: Sources of Light and Sound
indicators: Identify natural sources of light (sun) and artificial sources (bulb, torch, fire, candle)
Recognise that we see objects because of light
Identify sources of sound (voices, musical instruments, animals, machines)
Work in pairs to sort pictures of light and sound sources (collaboration)
Use digital resources to explore light and sound (digital literacy)
Appreciate the importance of light and sound in daily life (personal development)
sessions.content:
Bright and Loud – Light and Sound

Light helps us see. Sound helps us hear and communicate. Both come from different sources.

1. Light Sources

  • Natural light source: The sun is the main source of light on Earth. Fireflies also produce light.
  • Artificial light sources (man-made): Electric bulb, torchlight, candle, lantern, fire, car headlights.

We see objects because light from a source bounces off the object and enters our eyes.

2. Sound Sources

  • People and animals: talking, singing, barking, mooing, chirping.
  • Musical instruments: drum, bell, rattle, guitar, flute.
  • Machines and objects: car horn, ringing phone, school bell, falling object.

Sound is made when something vibrates (moves back and forth quickly). We hear sound with our ears.

Activity 1 – Light and sound hunt
Walk around the classroom and school compound. List all sources of light and sound you see and hear. Categorise them as natural or artificial. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Sound shakers
Make simple shakers from plastic bottles filled with seeds or stones. Shake them. Discuss: How is the sound made? (Vibration – the seeds hit the bottle). (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a digital interactive board where you tap on objects and hear their sounds or see if they emit light. (digital literacy).

Exercise 6.1

  1. Name the biggest natural source of light.
  2. Write two artificial sources of light you use at home.
  3. What is your favourite sound? Where does it come from?
  4. Draw a picture of a night scene showing two sources of light and label them.

sessions.title: Weather Elements – Sun, Rain, Wind, Clouds, Temperature
indicators: Identify different weather conditions: sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, hot, cold
Describe the weather for the day using simple terms
Relate weather to appropriate clothing and activities
Work in groups to maintain a weekly weather chart (collaboration)
Use a digital weather app or video to observe weather patterns (digital literacy)
Understand how weather affects our daily lives (personal development)
sessions.content:
What's the Weather? – Observing the Sky

Weather is the condition of the air outside at a particular time. It can be sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, hot or cold.

1. Types of Weather

  • Sunny: The sun shines brightly. The sky is clear. It feels warm or hot.
  • Rainy: Water falls from clouds. Sometimes with thunder and lightning. We use umbrellas.
  • Windy: The air moves strongly. Leaves fly, trees sway. We feel the breeze.
  • Cloudy: The sky is covered with clouds. It may look grey. The sun is hidden.
  • Hot: The temperature is high. We sweat. We wear light clothes.
  • Cold: The temperature is low. We feel chilly. We may wear a sweater or jacket. Harmattan is a cold, dry season in Ghana.

2. Seasons in Ghana

Ghana has two main seasons: the rainy season and the dry season (Harmattan). The rainy season is often from April to October. The dry season is from November to March.

Activity 1 – Weather reporter
Each morning, a pupil looks outside and reports the weather to the class: 'Today it is sunny and hot.' Record on a weekly chart with symbols. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Weather and clothes match
Show pictures of different weather. Pupils match them with appropriate clothing (e.g., raincoat for rainy, sweater for cold/harmattan). (creativity).

Digital corner: Check a simple weather forecast website or app. Compare the predicted weather with what you observe outside. (digital literacy).

Exercise 7.1

  1. Draw the symbol for a sunny day and a rainy day.
  2. What season is it now? How do you know?
  3. What clothes should you wear on a cold harmattan morning? Write a sentence.
  4. Why do we need to know the weather forecast? Give one reason.

sessions.title: Sources of Water and Its Importance
indicators: Identify natural and man-made sources of water: rain, river, stream, well, borehole, tap
List everyday uses of water: drinking, cooking, washing, farming, cleaning
Explain why clean water is essential for health
Work in pairs to create a poster on the uses of water (creativity, collaboration)
Watch a short digital video on the journey of water (digital literacy)
Develop habits of saving water and preventing pollution (personal development)
sessions.content:
Water Is Life – Where It Comes From and How We Use It

Water is very important. Every living thing needs water to survive. We get water from different sources.

1. Sources of Water

  • Rain: Water that falls from clouds. We can collect it in tanks or buckets.
  • River or stream: Natural flowing water. Many villages rely on rivers.
  • Well: A deep hole dug into the ground to reach underground water.
  • Borehole: A narrow, machine-drilled hole that brings water up with a pump.
  • Tap (pipe-borne water): Water supplied through pipes to homes and schools. Often treated and clean.

2. Uses of Water

  • Drinking: We need clean water to stay healthy and avoid diseases.
  • Cooking: Water is used to prepare rice, soup, banku, tea.
  • Washing: Bathing, washing clothes, washing dishes.
  • Farming: Watering plants and giving animals water to drink.
  • Cleaning: Mopping floors, flushing toilets.

Activity 1 – Water walk
Walk around the school compound. Identify all sources of water: tap, water barrel, puddle. Discuss where each came from. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Save water poster
In pairs, make a poster showing three ways to save water (e.g., turn off the tap while brushing teeth, use a cup to take water, fix leaking taps). Display. (creativity, collaboration).

Digital corner: Watch a short animated video about the water cycle or how water gets from a river to a tap. Discuss. (digital literacy).

Exercise 8.1

  1. Name two sources of water found in your community.
  2. Write three ways you use water every day.
  3. Why is it important to drink clean water?
  4. Draw one way you can save water at home and write a sentence about it.
